questions: Did this difficulty with sideways eye movements begin suddenly?
Has it been progressively worsening since it began?
Have you had this problem since childhood or early adulthood?
Are your voluntary up-and-down eye movements also impaired?
Can you follow a slowly moving object smoothly with your eyes?
Do your eyes move normally when you turn your head rapidly from side to side?
Do you experience visual blurring or the sensation that the world is moving?
Have you developed difficulty walking, frequent falls, or problems with balance?
Do you have poor coordination of your hands or limbs?
Has your speech become slurred or unusually slow?
Have you developed stiffness, slowed movements, tremor, or difficulty initiating walking?
Have you noticed changes in memory, judgment, behavior, or personality?
Have you had weakness, numbness, facial drooping, or difficulty speaking?
Have you had seizures, severe headaches, or episodes of loss of consciousness?
Did this begin after a head injury, stroke, infection, or exposure to a new medication or toxin?
Does anyone in your family have similar eye-movement, balance, or coordination problems?
Have you had unexplained weight loss, cancer, or a recent autoimmune illness?

results: 1. Bedside neuro-ophthalmic examination of saccades, smooth pursuit, optokinetic nystagmus, vestibulo-ocular reflex, convergence, and gaze-holding
nystagmus: direction and whether it changes with gaze: no nystagmus
smooth pursuit and saccades: ocular motor apraxia - failure to initiate voluntary horizontal saccades with compensatory head thrusts
vertical gaze and convergence: normal
head impulse test: normal - no corrective saccade
2. Video-oculography with quantitative horizontal and vertical saccade, pursuit, and vestibulo-ocular-reflex testing
video-oculography / eye-movement recording: failure to initiate voluntary horizontal saccades with compensatory head thrusts; ocular motor apraxia
smooth pursuit and saccades: ocular motor apraxia - failure to initiate voluntary horizontal saccades with compensatory head thrusts
3. Brain MRI with thin-section imaging of the cerebellum, brainstem, and cerebellar peduncles
MRI brain with gadolinium: cerebellar vermis hypoplasia with molar tooth sign; no abnormal enhancement
4. Comprehensive hereditary cerebellar ataxia and ocular-motor-apraxia genetic panel, including SETX, PNKP, APTX, and PNKD-related disorders
genetic testing (exome): pathogenic variants in ciliopathy genes on exome sequencing
5. Serum alpha-fetoprotein, albumin, immunoglobulins, and lymphocyte count
full blood count and biochemistry: normal
6. Serum vitamin E, copper, ceruloplasmin, thyroid function tests, vitamin B12, and folate
vitamin B12 with methylmalonic acid: normal
serum folate: normal
serum vitamin E: normal
serum copper and caeruloplasmin: normal
TSH / free T4: normal
7. Chromosomal microarray and examination for biallelic PNKP-related disease if the initial genetic panel is nondiagnostic
genetic testing (exome): pathogenic variants in ciliopathy genes on exome sequencing
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Joubert syndrome (a developmental ciliopathy with cerebellar vermis hypoplasia and molar tooth sign), caused by pathogenic variants in a Joubert-associated ciliopathy gene

Alternative: Ataxia with oculomotor apraxia due to a recessive DNA-repair disorder, particularly AOA1 or AOA2

Alternative: Congenital ocular motor apraxia with cerebellar vermis hypoplasia

Alternative: Poretti–Boltshauser syndrome due to biallelic LAMA1 variants
